abstract: For an $n \times n$ $(0,1)$-matrix $A$ with row and column sum $k$, a perfect partition of the set $\mathcal{P}_A$ of permutation matrices dominated by $A$ is a partition of $\mathcal{P}_A$ into $k$-element subsets each summing to $A$. For the derangement matrix $L_n = J_n - I_n$ (the regular bipartite graph $L_{n,1} = K_{n,n} - I_{n,n}$), Brualdi, Chiang, and Li (2005) settled $n \le 5$ and asked in Problems 3.2 and 3.3 whether $\mathcal{P}_{L_n}$, the even derangements $\mathcal{P}_{L_n} \cap \mathcal{A}_n$, or fixed cycle-type classes admit perfect partitions for $n \ge 6$. Li, Soosiah, and Yu (2012) resolved $\mathcal{P}_{L_6}$, and Ferreri, Parameswaran, and Yu (2026) resolved $\mathcal{P}_{L_7}$ and prime $p$-cycles while leaving $n \ge 8$ open. Using a subgroup-orbit criterion (Lemma 3.1) that reduces $H$-conjugation-invariant perfect partitions to exact cover on $H$-orbits, we resolve these questions through $n = 9$: we construct $\operatorname{PGL}(2,7)$- and $\operatorname{P\Gamma L}(2,8)$-invariant perfect partitions of $L_{8,1}$ and $L_{9,1}$ and an $\operatorname{AGL}(1,7)$-invariant partition of $L_{7,1}$ (Theorem 1.1); we construct perfect partitions of $\mathcal{P}_{L_n} \cap \mathcal{A}_n$ for $6 \le n \le 9$ (Theorem 1.2); we classify pure cycle-type perfect partitions at $n = 6, 7$, constructing partitions for $(4,2)$ at $n = 6$ and $(5,2), (4,3)$ at $n = 7$ and proving impossibility for $(6), (3,3), (2,2,2)$ at $n = 6$ and $(3,2,2)$ at $n = 7$ (Theorem 1.3); and we prove that $\mathcal{P}_{L_6} \setminus \mathcal{A}_6$ has no perfect partition and $L_{6,1}$ has no $\operatorname{PGL}(2,5)$-invariant perfect partition (Proposition 1.4). All constructions and finite enumerations for $n \le 9$ are verified by standalone scripts; general orders $n \ge 10$ remain open.
author: lihongmin
change_summary:
- (1) Corrected the maximum pairwise disjoint packing number of pure (2,2,2) perfect sets at n = 6 from 2 to 1 in the Section 1.2 summary table, Theorem 1.3(1), and Section 5.1 (each of the 15 unordered pairs among the 6 sets intersects in 1 involution), added the standalone standard-library script supplement/verify_packing.py (also invoked by supplement/verify_all.py) to verify this pairwise intersection structure, the n = 6 (3,3) max pairwise disjoint permutation bound (4), and the n = 4 perfect-set cycle-type breakdown, and updated Section 6, supplement/README.md, and supplement/CONTENTS.sha256 accordingly.
- (2) Narrowed Remark 4.1 by removing the inference that multi-orbit blocks covering the remaining 28 regular PGL(2,7)-orbits at n = 8 must mix cycle types, stating only that they require multiple H-orbits (r >= 2).
- (3) Corrected two descriptions of prior work: in Sections 1.1, 1.2 (summary table), and 2(1), noted that the n = 4 partition in [1, Proposition 3.1] mixes one (2,2)-involution with two 4-cycles in each block (whereas n = 2, 3, 5 partition each cycle type separately), and rewrote Remark 5.1 to state the n = 4 discrepancy in [1, p. 72] directly without speculative interpretation; in Sections 1.1 and 2(3), described the computational method of [3, Section 4.4] as randomized greedy search followed by a hybrid of Algorithm X and the Bron-Kerbosch clique-finding algorithm rather than integer programming.
- (4) Added an explanation in Section 5.1 of why the first-image backtracking enumeration visits every perfect set in a candidate pool once and only once (completeness and non-redundancy), explicitly labeled which structural assertions in Sections 4.3 and 5 are established by complete enumeration (and added explicit verification of opposite 3-cycle orientations and distinct complementary matchings for all 840 pure (3,2,2) sets at n = 7 in supplement/verify_all.py), added a concise description of subgroup selection and candidate-block generation in Section 4.1, moved repeated orbit-size and stabilizer-order inventories out of the statements of Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 and Proposition 1.4 into Sections 4.2 and 5.1-5.3, and shortened the abstract.
title: Perfect Partitions of Derangements and Even Derangements for $n \le 9$
